body: > I simply eyeballed some different lighting setups, and got all of them to look right using these factors Lights match perfectly between Blender and Godot in non-physical mode if you export in Unitless mode, there's no need to eyeball.

I agree with this but there are compatibility considerations discussed [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11842)

This should be changed in both blend and gltf importer simultaneously because those two are basically the same and should behave identically on import (I mean all changes to light import, not just attenuation)
Ah, yeah. That's probably better to do in another PR then, rather keep this one focused on the very obvious issue of the light energy/intensity values.

Not sure if it is actually, the discussion in that proposal was about changing the default value in nodes which would immediately break existing projects. But this PR changes import logic, not the default. Strictly speaking it's already breaking import compatibility by changing light intensity, so maybe it makes sense to fix the attenuation as well
So they do! I tried that, but I suppose there was something else wrong in that version, haha. This is much better, fixed in d3dfcea9b73dab3ce3b0657c3da73b4bb4691ed6.

I moved the attenuation fix to apply to all glTF imports, that seems like an obvious enough fix (assuming that changing import results isn't breaking): ee9ebe4a850e685fa9efc7eed8efe1a23742fbd3

I would rather not generalize the light brightness fix to all glTFs, because the luminous efficacy constant used to convert Blender watts into glTF lumens is a less clear specification issue (see #73624), which as far as I know, used to be (is?) 683, and is now in the process of being changed to 177.82 (which has a better logic behind it, I think). This PR's intention is to try and fix this specifically for Blender files, because Blender is not a moving target unlike the glTF specification, we can just look at what Blender uses for luminous efficacy.

~~Though I suppose that specifically for projects using non-physical light units, all glTFs could be imported using the Unitless lighting mode, now that that's apparently all that's needed.~~ Nevermind, that's too late, it's a Blender option, not a glTF option, it's just up to the glTF author to export using Unitless and it'll work fine with non-physical light units :smile:

Turns out they ended up a bit brighter than Blender when comparing default exposure to default exposure (see updated screenshots), but I think that's very acceptable given how simple of a fix this was. (The MRP screenshot looks the worst, but maybe it's fine, if this is a common workflow anyway.)
Should we do anything with this value on export? We want to ensure that if a glTF file is exported from Godot, it will be imported again with at least roughly the same appearance.

I checked [the glTF lights spec](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_lights_punctual/README.md) just now, and I don't think there is any field in the glTF lights that would replicate the effect of this parameter. Technically the falloff isn't even specified very strictly, it's more like a recommendation in [the range section](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/blob/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_lights_punctual/README.md#range-property).

The intensity of the light could be tweaked somehow based on the attenuation to get some lights looking a bit more correct, but it's never going to look right across different intensities with a different falloff function, so I'd rather not.
